transcript.text: w/m finally died after 12 yrs, whats the best one to buy under £400? family of 5

On buying: I can't vouch for specific models, prices or stock, but here's what matters for a family of five on under £400. 1. Capacity: go for 9kg, or 10kg if it fits the budget. 7–8kg machines struggle with bedding and big family loads, so you end up running more cycles.
2. Motor: an inverter (brushless) motor is quieter, usually more reliable, and often comes with a longer motor warranty.
3. 4. Running costs: with that many washes, a better energy rating pays back over the years. A good 30–40 minute quick wash and a decent 20°C/eco programme are worth having.
5. Warranty and parts: brands with good UK parts support (Bosch, Samsung, LG, Hotpoint, Beko and Hisense all sit around this price) are easier to repair later. A 2–5 year warranty is a good tie-breaker.
6. Fit: measure the space, especially the depth. 9–10kg machines are often deeper. Before you spend £400, it's worth five minutes to rule out the simple things. Sometimes a machine that seems dead is nothing serious. At 12 years old, though, if it turns out to be the motor, main board or bearings, replacing it is usually the sensible call. 1. Power: plug something else into the same socket, and if you're confident, swap the 13A fuse in the plug. If it then comes to life, the machine was fine all along.
2. Locks: check for a padlock or key symbol (child lock) and that the door is shut firmly until it clicks. Buttons that do nothing, or a door that won't lock, can stop it starting.
3. Water and drain: make sure the tap behind it is on. Then, with it unplugged and towels down, open the small filter at the bottom front and clear any fluff, coins or grips. A blocked filter can stop a cycle partway through. If none of that helps, tell me exactly what it does now and I'll tell you honestly whether it's worth repairing.

it stopped mid-cycle 2 days ago with water still in the drum. won't drain or spin, just hums when it tries to drain. some lights flashing too. didn't know there was a filter. if repair is cheap id do it

That's a much more hopeful picture. A machine that stops with water in the drum, won't spin and hums when it tries to drain usually has a drain problem, not a dead motor. It won't spin until it has emptied, and the flashing lights are very likely its drain-fault warning. 1. Something blocking the pump filter or caught in the pump just behind it, like fluff, a coin, a hair grip or a baby sock. It's a free fix.
2. A kinked or blocked drain hose, or a blocked standpipe or sink waste where it empties.
3. The drain pump itself has jammed or worn out. Humming with no water moving can mean a failed pump, but a blockage makes exactly the same sound, so rule that out first. On cost: clearing the filter costs nothing. If it does turn out to be the pump, that's normally one of the cheaper washing machine repairs, and on many machines it's a reasonable DIY job. So it's well worth checking before you buy a new one. 1. Get ready for water. There could be several litres in the drum. Lay down plenty of towels and find a baking tray or other shallow dish that fits under the front. Open the small flap or kick-plate at the bottom front. Many machines have a thin emergency drain tube beside the filter. If yours does, pull it out, unplug its end over the tray and let the water out in stages.
2. Once the flow slows, unscrew the filter slowly, about a quarter turn at a time, so more water can trickle out. Then take it out fully and clean it. If you find debris, that's very likely your culprit.
3. With the filter out, shine a torch into the opening and turn the small plastic impeller with a finger. If it spins freely, the pump isn't jammed. If it's stuck, feel for anything wedged in it. Broken or cracked vanes point to the pump.
4. Refit the filter firmly and straight. Then pull the machine out a little and check the grey drain hose at the back isn't kinked or crushed. Then plug it in and run a drain or spin-only programme. If it still hums and nothing moves, even with a clear filter, a free-turning impeller and a straight hose, the pump is the prime suspect, and we can talk about whether to replace it. Let me know what you find in the f
ok will try the filter. water still in the drum so unplugging first. will report back

Unplugging first is exactly right. A couple of tips before you start: 1. Expect more water than you think. A drum that stopped mid-cycle can hold quite a few litres, so drain it in small batches into a shallow tray and close the filter (or plug the emergency tube) between batches.
2. Wear rubber gloves if you have them. Water that's sat for two days can smell pretty grim, and there may be bits in the filter.
3. Once it's out, have a feel for the impeller in the opening as well. Freely turning, jammed and broken vanes each point somewhere different.
4. When you refit the filter, screw it in fully and straight with its rubber seal clean. A filter cap that isn't seated properly is a common cause of a leak afterwards. When you report back, tell me:
• what was in the filter (clear, something you removed, or a blockage you couldn't shift)
• whether the impeller turns freely
• what happens on a drain or spin-only programme afterwards: does the water pump away, or does it still just hum? That will tell us whether it was a free fix, the hose, or the pump.
ok, got the tray and towels. will check the filter and the impeller and let you know what happens

Sounds like you're well set up. Just a few extra pointers in case things don't go smoothly: 1. If the filter is very stiff, grip it with a rubber glove or a cloth for extra purchase, but don't lever it with a screwdriver. Old plastic caps can crack.
2. If water barely trickles out of the emergency tube or round the filter, something may be packed right against it. That actually points towards a blockage, so keep going slowly.
3. If you lose track and water is coming faster than the tray can take, just screw the filter back in a turn, empty the tray and carry on. When you're done, tell me what was in the filter, whether the impeller turns freely, and what happens on a drain or spin-only run. If it pumps away, it was a free fix. If it still just hums with everything clear, we'll look at the hose and then the pump.
ok, doing it now. will report back once done

Good luck, take it slowly and you'll be fine. One small extra tip for afterwards: if the lights are still flashing once the filter is back in, leave it unplugged for a minute or two before you plug it back in and select a drain or spin-only programme. That clears the old fault so it gets a fresh try at draining. When you're done, just let me know three things: what was in the filter, whether the impeller turned freely, and whether the water pumped away or it still just hummed. That'll tell us whether it's sorted, or whether the hose or the pump is next on the list.
ok, filter's out, still sorting it. will report back

You're doing well. While the filter's out, here are two things worth knowing: 1. Before you refit it, reach gently into the opening with a gloved finger. Coins, grips and wads of fluff can sit further back than the filter itself, right against the pump.
2. When you turn the impeller, a little notchy or stepped resistance is normal on many pumps, because the magnet inside moves in steps. What matters is whether it goes round. Completely solid, or cracked or missing vanes, would point to the pump. When you're done, let me know what was in there and how the impeller felt. Then we'll see what happens on a drain or spin run.
ok bit of a mess here. water's out, filter's out, still checking the impeller. will report back

A bit of mess is par for the course, and getting the water out is the hardest part done. While the machine's still unplugged with the filter out, there's one extra quick test that's worth doing, especially if the filter and impeller both turn out clean. 1. Keep the tray and towels in place under the filter opening.
2. Pour a jug of water (a litre or so) into the drum through the door.
3. Watch the filter opening. If the water gushes out quickly, the path from the drum down to the pump is clear. If it only trickles or nothing comes out, something is stuck in the internal hose between the drum and the pump, often a sock or small item of clothing. That would explain the symptoms even with a perfectly good pump. So here's where that leaves us:
• Something found in the filter or wedged at the impeller: very likely the whole cause, and it should drain once it's refitted.
• Filter clean, impeller turns freely, jug water flows out well: the drain hose at the back or the pump itself becomes the main suspect, and the drain or spin test afterwards will tell us which.
• Impeller solid or vanes broken: that points to the drain pump. When you're ready, let me know what was in the filter, how the impeller felt, and how the jug water came through.
ok, impeller checking still. havent got a jug test result yet. will report back

No rush. Take your time with it. 1. What was in the filter: clean, something you pulled out, or a blockage you couldn't shift.
2. How the impeller felt: turns round (even if a bit notchy), completely solid, or vanes cracked or missing.
3. The jug test, if you get to it: water gushing out of the opening, or only a trickle.
Even just the first two will narrow it down a lot. Something found at the filter or impeller usually means it's sorted. A solid or broken impeller points to the drain pump. If everything's clear, we'll check the hoses next.
